title: That you may know (1 John 5)
hookLine: the letter ends: little children, keep yourselves from idols

lines: THE POINT, SAVED FOR THE END.
cards: Some letters bury the point in the middle. This one saves it for the end. In the last chapter, the writer gives what some readers take as his reason for writing all of it.
And he signs off with a line that seems to come out of nowhere. Not grace be with you. Not peace.
Just this: little children, keep yourselves from idols. No explanation, and then amen.

teach.b: The chapter opens with love in practice. In the King James Bible: "For this is the love of God, that we keep his commandments: and his commandments are not grievous." Not grievous: not a crushing load.
And: "this is the victory that overcometh the world, even our faith."

teach.h: WRITTEN SO YOU CAN KNOW, NOT GUESS.
teach.b: Then the purpose of the whole letter, in verse thirteen: "These things have I written unto you that believe on the name of the Son of God; that ye may know that ye have eternal life."
That ye may know: not hope, not guess, not lie awake wondering. Some readers hear the Greek verb as settled knowing, the kind you don't keep checking.
After page after page of tests, you might expect anxiety; the writer says he wrote so they could stop wondering and rest. A note for anyone comparing Bibles.
In the King James Bible, verse seven has a line about three that bear record in heaven: the Father, the Word and the Holy Ghost.

Some modern translations leave that line out or put it in a footnote, and their notes explain why. Churches that teach the Trinity draw it from many passages and the early creeds, not from this one verse.
Then the ending: "Little children, keep yourselves from idols." Scholars aren't sure what he had in mind. Maybe the temple statues in a city like Ephesus, where tradition places the elder.
Maybe the false pictures of God the letter has warned about.
Maybe anything that quietly takes God's place. The letter doesn't say. It leaves the line ringing, like a parent calling after you at the door: take care of yourselves.

how: Some Christians read 1 John 5:13 as a word of assurance, and in teaching and preaching the letter's last line about idols is sometimes applied to anything, not only statues, that takes God's place in a life.

games.q: you're the elder, finishing a long letter to people you love. what's your last line?
o: warm greetings from the whole church.
little children, keep yourselves from idols.
games.why: no greetings, no summary: "little children, keep yourselves from idols." he leaves it unexplained.

practice: In the wider sense some Christian teachers use, an idol is anything sitting in the center where something truer belongs: your phone, someone's approval, money, a grudge, a plan for how life has to go.
Name one gently, like a houseguest who has stayed too long, and let each breath move it an inch from the center. If you pray, rest on the old line from Psalm 46: be still, and know that I am God.

wordCard.voice: Idols. The strange parting shot that ends First John: keep yourselves from idols, after a letter written so its readers could know, not guess, that they have life.

orig.note: Greek: that you may know, from oida, to know. it's the verb in 1 John 5:13.

carryVoice: Your line: keep yourselves from idols. A parting word, like a parent's at the door. See you tomorrow.
